source.title: Elucidating and Overcoming the Challenges of Label Noise in Supervised Contrastive Learning
source.authors: Zijun Long; George Killick; Li-Peng Zhuang; R. Mccreadie; G. Aragon-Camarasa; Paul Henderson

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and supplementary material; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests supervised contrastive learning on synthetic noisy-label datasets, a new setting for the claim. It reports test accuracy by noise level but does not measure training error.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on noisy labels, but not random labels, shuffled or noise inputs, training error, training time, or the order in which real and noisy labels are learned. The reported dataset error-rate estimates and pair-similarity analyses concern label noise and contrastive pairs, not the claim versions' fitting outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates label-noise mitigation and downstream classification accuracy. It does not measure memorization, training-set fit, or learning order. Table 4's test-accuracy decline alone does not test V4's claim that networks fit corrupted training labels perfectly while retaining signal. The original random-label finding is cited as background, rather than used as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that D-SCL mitigates annotation-error bias and improves downstream classification when training from scratch or fine-tuning, especially under realistic low-to-moderate noise. At 40% noise, its performance falls behind Sel-CL and TCL. They do not conclude that their networks memorize random labels.
record.recipe_differences: Studies supervised contrastive learning with several objectives and synthetic label noise; it does not use the original random-label intervention or measure training error.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise level and dataset change test accuracy; at higher synthetic noise rates D-SCL loses relative performance to Sel-CL and TCL.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 4 reports downstream test accuracy for five training objectives at clean, 18%, and 40% noise settings. Every reported method has lower accuracy at higher noise; none of R12, R15, or R20 reverses that trend. Training-set fit is unreported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise reduces downstream classification accuracy in these BEiT-3 experiments, with the size of the decline depending on the training objective.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections 4 and 8 analyze pair-label errors and embedding-similarity distributions, while the remaining experiments compare mitigation objectives and their ablations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human annotation errors create false-positive contrastive pairs whose embedding similarities overlap those of true positives; debiasing these pairs can improve downstream classification.

record.problems: The noise robustness experiment measures classification accuracy, not training error; it tests only Clean, 18%, and 40% label-noise settings on CIFAR-10N and Clean and 40% on CIFAR-100N. The study identifies these labels as synthetic and not predominantly naturally arising human errors. Results are means across three initializations overall, but no uncertainty estimates are reported for Table 4.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit real and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions. Claims of mitigation efficiency do not measure these.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training-set fit across corruption fractions, progressive degradation toward chance over the none-to-all range, and simultaneous signal learning and noise memorization. The reported mitigation benchmarks do not establish these outcomes.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing those regularizers.
Temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: The extracted Table 4 values match the supplied text. All are mean Top-1 test accuracies over three initializations, without reported uncertainty. The paper describes CIFAR-N noise as predominantly synthetic, but does not specify a random-corruption mechanism here; that description alone cannot establish the random-label intervention required by the claims.

versions.untested_parts: Random labeling, training error, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time and convergence speed as corrupted-label fraction changes.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Training-set fit or training error; test error at 100% corrupted labels; whether test error rises steadily through the full range from none to all. The reported test-accuracy results by label-noise level are extracted below, but cannot establish the full version.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.
